title: A guest enters like fire
theme: At Yama’s house, after three nights without welcome, the household tells Yama: a brāhmaṇa guest is fire itself; bring water.

words.meaning: Vaiśvānara, the fire (common to all men)

words.context: Śaṅkara: the welcome of water for the feet, a seat and the like

sandhi.type: iḥ before a voiced consonant; aḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: iḥ → ir before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः); aḥ → o before g, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

sandhi_exceptions.note: The base prints praviśati atithiḥ with the vowels unjoined; the vishvAsa mūla, Madhva’s text and Raṅgarāmānuja write praviśaty atithiḥ (corrections.json). The count of the anuṣṭubh (16) is the same either way.

morphology.note: Vṛddhi derivative of viśvānara, ‘belonging to all men’: the fire, especially as the sacrificial and digestive fire.
gṛha is often plural in the sense ‘a house, a household’.

translation.literal: As Vaiśvānara a brāhmaṇa guest enters houses; for him they make this appeasement. Bring water, O Vaivasvata!
translation.readable: ‘A brāhmaṇa who comes as a guest enters a house like fire itself; people calm him with this welcome. Bring water, son of Vivasvat!’

anvaya: ब्राह्मणः अतिथिः वैश्वानरः [सन्] गृहान् प्रविशति । तस्य [सन्तः] एताम् शान्तिम् कुर्वन्ति । [अतः] वैवस्वत, उदकम् हर ॥
syntax: A general statement (a guest enters as fire), a second about custom (people appease him), and an imperative addressed to Yama. The speakers are not named in the verse.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: Yama’s ministers or wife — «अमात्या भार्या वा ऊचुर्बोधयन्तः». Raṅgarāmānuja: the elders at the door. Madhva’s cited verse and his sub-commentators: Yama’s wife, who had offered the welcome that the boy would not accept while Yama was away.

ambiguities.topic: What happened in the three nights?
ambiguities.note: The verse does not narrate it; Śaṅkara supplies it: the boy went to Yama’s house and stayed three nights while Yama was away — «स च यमभवनं गत्वा तिस्रो रात्रीरुवास यमे प्रोषिते». Madhva’s verse adds that he refused the wife’s hospitality.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: A regular anuṣṭubh, 16 + 16 syllables as written (with the unjoined hiatus).

beginner: The scene jumps. The boy has gone to the house of Death, but Death was away. For three nights he waited without food. When Death returns, his household warns him: a brāhmaṇa guest who enters a house is like fire. If he is not welcomed, he burns the house; welcomed, he is calmed. So bring water to wash his feet, quickly! In ancient India the guest was sacred, almost a god. Leaving a guest unfed was a serious wrong, even for Death himself. The verse turns the situation around: the boy who was given away to Death has become Death’s honoured guest, and Death is now in his debt.
analogy: Like a powerful official who returns home to find an important visitor has been kept waiting in the hall for days, and whose staff whisper urgently: attend to him at once.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: A brāhmaṇa guest enters a house as fire; people appease him with this welcome; bring water, son of Vivasvat.

commentary.q: Why is the guest called fire?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the guest is fire itself, entering as if to burn — «वैश्वानरः अग्निरेव साक्षात् प्रविशति अतिथिः सन् ब्राह्मणः गृहान् दहन्निव» — and the welcome quiets that burning. Raṅgarāmānuja gives the household’s fear in their own words: «तदपचारेण दग्धा मा भूम», let us not be burned by slighting him.

commentary.q: What does the Dvaita tradition add?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva cites a verse that fills in the story: «स जगाम यमं बालो ब्रह्मचारी यमस्य तु», the boy went to Yama, and though honoured by Yama’s wife did not accept her welcome; when Yama came she said «आगते तु यमे प्राह यमं सोदकमाहर». A later Dvaita commentator on Madhva, Vāmanapaṇḍita, takes vaiśvānara as Viṣṇu dwelling in all men (not quoted here).

advaita.text: The guest is fire; the welcome is a ‘quieting’ of fire: «वैश्वानरः अग्निरेव साक्षात्».

visistadvaita.text: The elders warn Yama, for fear of being burned by the slight: «तदपचारेण दग्धा मा भूम».

dvaita.text: Yama’s wife speaks, the boy having refused her welcome: «आगते तु यमे प्राह यमं सोदकमाहर». (Vāmanapaṇḍita, commenting on Madhva, reads vaiśvānara as Viṣṇu in all men.)

schools.disagreement: The schools differ on who speaks (ministers or wife, elders, the wife) and Vāmanapaṇḍita’s reading of vaiśvānara as Viṣṇu goes beyond the others’ ‘fire’.

parallels.note: The Taittirīya’s instruction to the departing student, ‘let the guest be a god to you’, states as a rule the reverence the Kaṭha dramatises.

contemporary.text: Even the most powerful owe basic courtesy to whoever comes to their door. The story makes Death himself the host who failed and must make amends. This is a modern reflection, not the text’s claim.

reflect.beginner: How do you treat someone who arrives when it is inconvenient?
reflect.deeper: Why might a tradition treat hospitality as something close to sacred?
reflect.practice: Welcome the next person who interrupts you as if their visit mattered.

flags.note: The base prints praviśati atithiḥ unjoined; the vishvAsa mūla and Madhva’s text join it (corrections.json).
